Horsemen
HORS-men
n. pl.
From horse and man. Webster 1828: a rider on horseback; a man skilled in riding; and, in the plural, cavalry, mounted troops. In Scripture horsemen are the arm of war a nation is most tempted to trust, and the title Elisha gave to a single praying prophet.

Biblical Definition

Horsemen are the cavalry, the fastest and most feared arm of ancient war, and Scripture uses them chiefly to expose misplaced confidence. Pharaoh’s horses and chariots… and his horsemen, and his army pursued Israel to the sea and drowned there (Exodus 14:9). Isaiah pronounces the woe: Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD! (Isaiah 31:1). The indictment is not that horsemen are useless but that Judah looked to them and not to God. The psalm states the alternative in a line every believer should know: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God (Psalm 20:7). Then comes the reversal that gives the word its glory. As Elijah went up in the whirlwind, Elisha cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof (2 Kings 2:12) — the real cavalry of the nation was one man who prayed. The same words were spoken over Elisha’s own deathbed by the king (2 Kings 13:14). And his servant, hemmed in at Dothan, was shown the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HORSEMAN as a rider on horseback; a man skilled in riding; and a mounted soldier — the plural denoting cavalry. The military sense is the biblical one throughout.

expand to see more

HORSEMAN, n. — A rider on horseback; one who is skilled in riding.

A mounted soldier; a trooper; in the plural, cavalry.

HORSEMANSHIP, n. — The act or art of riding, and of training and managing horses.

The law forbade the king of Israel to multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to that end (Deuteronomy 17:16).

That prohibition is the background to Isaiah 31:1 and to Solomon’s importation of horses from Egypt in 1 Kings 10:28-29.

Key Scripture

Exodus 14:9 — "But the Egyptians pursued after them, all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, and his horsemen, and his army, and overtook them encamping by the sea, beside Pihahiroth, before Baalzephon."

Isaiah 31:1 — "Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!"

Psalm 20:7 — "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God."

2 Kings 2:12 — "And Elisha saw it, and he cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no more: and he took hold of his own clothes, and rent them in two pieces."

2 Kings 6:17 — "And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 31:1 is not a warning against armies but against the direction of a nation’s gaze, and the modern equivalents — the reserves, the platform, the institution, the plan — produce exactly the same woe.

expand to see more

Judah’s error was not that she armed but that she went down to Egypt for help and did not look unto the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah’s indictment turns entirely on the last clause: they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD. The horses and chariots were real, the Egyptians were genuinely strong, and the whole calculation was sound in every respect except the one that mattered. Scripture never treats prudence as sin — Nehemiah set a watch and prayed, and the law regulated an army. What it forbids is the transfer of trust, and the transfer is nearly always invisible, because the outward arrangements of the faithless and the faithful look almost identical. Psalm 20:7 gives the test: what does a man remember when the day of battle comes.

Elisha’s cry supplies the doctrine positively and should be preached where the church is anxious about its strength. My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof — the nation’s real defence, in the prophet’s estimate, was the old man being carried up in the whirlwind, not the standing army of the northern kingdom. A generation later the king of Israel wept the identical words over Elisha’s deathbed. And when the Syrian host surrounded Dothan and the servant despaired, the prophet prayed and the young man saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. The invisible cavalry was always there. What the servant needed was not reinforcements but opened eyes.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew parash (H6571), a horseman or a horse for riding; sus (H5483), a horse; rekeb (H7393), a chariot; Greek hippeus (G2460), a horseman.

expand to see more

Hebrew parash (H6571) — a horseman, a rider; also used of the horse itself in some passages.

Hebrew sus (H5483) — a horse; some trust in chariots, and some in horses (Psalm 20:7).

Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — a chariot, or chariotry collectively; Elisha’s chariot of Israel.

Hebrew Qadosh Yisrael — the Holy One of Israel; Isaiah’s characteristic title for God, used thirty times in his book.

Greek hippeus (G2460) — a horseman; Acts 23:23, 32, of the escort that took Paul to Caesarea.

Usage

"Trust in chariots… and in horsemen, because they are very strong (Isaiah 31:1) — a sound calculation with God omitted."

"Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember (Psalm 20:7) — the test is what a man remembers."

"The chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof (2 Kings 2:12) — a nation’s real cavalry was one praying man."
